==Problem 20==

Three different pairs of shoes are placed in a row so that no left shoe is next to a
right shoe from a different pair. In how many ways can these six shoes be lined up?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 60 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 72 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 90 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 108 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 120</imath>

==Solution 1==

Let <imath>A_R, A_L, B_R, B_L, C_R, C_L</imath> denote the shoes.


There are <imath>6</imath> ways to choose the first shoe. WLOG, assume it is <imath>A_R</imath>. We have <imath>A_R,</imath> __, __, __, __, __.


<imath>~~~~~</imath> Case <imath>1</imath>: The next shoe in line is <imath>A_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, A_L,</imath> __, __, __, __. Now, the next shoe in line must be either <imath>B_L</imath> or <imath>C_L</imath>. There are <imath>2</imath> ways to choose which one, but assume WLOG that it is <imath>B_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, A_L, B_L,</imath> __, __, __.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Subcase <imath>1</imath>: The next shoe in line is <imath>B_R</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, A_L, B_L, B_R,</imath> __, __. The only way to finish is <imath>A_R, A_L, B_L, B_R, C_R, C_L</imath>.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Subcase <imath>2</imath>: The next shoe in line is <imath>C_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, A_L, B_L, C_L,</imath> __, __. The only way to finish is <imath>A_R, A_L, B_L, C_L, C_R, B_R</imath>.


<imath>~~~~~</imath> In total, this case has <imath>(6)(2)(1 + 1) = 24</imath> orderings.


<imath>~~~~~</imath> Case <imath>2</imath>: The next shoe in line is either <imath>B_R</imath> or <imath>C_R</imath>. There are <imath>2</imath> ways to choose which one, but assume WLOG that it is <imath>B_R</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, B_R,</imath> __, __, __, __.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Subcase <imath>1</imath>: The next shoe is <imath>B_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, B_R, B_L,</imath> __, __, __.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Sub-subcase <imath>1</imath>: The next shoe in line is <imath>A_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, B_R, B_L, A_L,</imath> __, __. The only way to finish is <imath>A_R, B_R, B_L, A_L, C_L, C_R</imath>.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Sub-subcase <imath>2</imath>: The next shoe in line is <imath>C_L</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, B_R, B_L, C_L,</imath> __, __. The remaining shoes are <imath>C_R</imath> and <imath>A_L</imath>, but these shoes cannot be next to each other, so this sub-subcase is impossible.


<imath>~~~~~ ~~~~~</imath> Subcase <imath>2</imath>: The next shoe is <imath>C_R</imath>. We have <imath>A_R, B_R, C_R,</imath> __, __, __. The next shoe in line must be <imath>C_L</imath>, so we have <imath>A_R, B_R, C_R, C_L,</imath> __, __. There are <imath>2</imath> ways to finish, which are <imath>A_R, B_R, C_R, C_L, A_L, B_L</imath> and <imath>A_R, B_R, C_R, C_L, B_L, A_L</imath>.


<imath>~~~~~</imath> In total, this case has <imath>(6)(2)(1 + 2) = 36</imath> orderings.


Our final answer is <imath>24 + 36 = \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 60}</imath>

==Solution 2 (Tree Diagram)==
Label the pairs \( (L_1, R_1) \), \( (L_2, R_2) \), and \( (L_3, R_3) \).

We now create a tree diagram. [[WLOG]], we say our first tree diagram starts with \( L_1 \).

[[File:2024 AMC 10B Q20.png | center | 500px]]

This tree has 10 branches.

Notice how we can interchange the first shoe with any \( L_1 \), \( L_2 \), \( L_3 \), \( R_1 \), \( R_2 \), \( R_3 \), and still get the same tree, but just interchanged shoes. Therefore, we just multiply the tree's branches by 6, to get \( 6 \cdot 10 =  \) <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 60}</imath>.

==Solution 3 (Fakesolve, Refer to Solution 4)==
We have two main cases: 

'''Case 1:''' <imath>LLLRRR</imath> or <imath>RRRLLL</imath> 

There are <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways to assign the shoes to the ordering. For now we'll focus on the <imath>LLLRRR</imath> case and multiply by <imath>2</imath> since they're symmetrical. WLOG say we have <imath>A_LB_LC_LC_RA_RB_R</imath>. We can flip <imath>A_L</imath> and <imath>B_L</imath> among themselves and <imath>A_R</imath> and <imath>B_R</imath> among themselves, so we get <imath>6 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 24.</imath> Multiplying by <imath>2</imath> for symmetry gives us <imath>48</imath> ways for this case. 



'''Case 2:''' <imath>RRLLLR</imath> or <imath>RLLLRR</imath> 

Again, we'll focus on the <imath>RRLLLR</imath> case and multiply by <imath>2</imath> since they're symmetrical. WLOG say we have <imath>B_RA_RA_LB_LC_LC_R</imath>. We can assign the shoes to the ordering in <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways. <imath>B_R</imath> can also be moved over to be next to <imath>C_R</imath>. Then we would have <imath>A_RA_LB_LC_LC_RB_R</imath>, which is also valid. So this case gives us <imath>6 \cdot 2 = 12</imath> ways. 

The answer is <imath>48 + 12 = \boxed{60}.</imath> 


~[[User:grogg007|grogg007]], ~EaZ_Shadow WWW

==Solution 4(focus on restrictions)==

Notice that you cannot have <imath>LRL</imath> or <imath>RLR</imath> in a row, since you are guaranteed an <imath>R</imath> and an <imath>L</imath> from a different pair. This means you can either have three <imath>L</imath>'s in a row, three <imath>R</imath>'s in a row, or you have two <imath>R</imath>'s between two <imath>L</imath>'s and two <imath>L</imath>'s between two <imath>R</imath>'s. 

Below are the cases(note that once an <imath>L</imath> is fixed the <imath>R</imath> adjacent to it is also fixed due to the constraint):
\begin{align*}
LLLRRR \Rightarrow 3!\cdot 2!=12\\
RLLLRR \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
RRLLLR \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
RRRLLL \Rightarrow 3!\cdot 2!=12\\
LRRRLL \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
LLRRRL \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
LRRLLR \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
RLLRRL \Rightarrow 3!=6\\
\end{align*}

We have <imath>2\cdot 12+6\cdot 6=\boxed{\textbf{(A) }60}.</imath>

~nevergonnagiveup

==Solution 5(for some reason this works)==

Let the pairs be <imath>L_1 R_1, L_2 R_2, L_3 R_3</imath>. The only ones that don't work are

<imath>L_1 R_2, L_1 R_3, L_2 R_1, L_2 R_3, L_3 R_2, L_3 R_1</imath> and their swaps so a total of <imath>12</imath> pairs that can't be in the string of <imath>6</imath>. We have <imath>6! = 720</imath> total ways and since there are <imath>12</imath> ways it won't work we simply do

<imath>\frac{720}{12} = \boxed{60}</imath>

==Solution 6==
Let <imath>A_1, A_2, A_3, B_1, B_2, B_3</imath> be the shoes. Initially, let's assume that it doesn't matter whether shoes of type <imath>A</imath> are left/right or if shoes of type <imath>B</imath> are left/right. We can have four possible arrangements: <imath>AAABBB</imath>, <imath>AABBBA</imath>, <imath>ABBAAB</imath>, and <imath>ABBBAA</imath>. Note that whenever we have a shoe of type <imath>A</imath> and a shoe of type <imath>B</imath> next to each other, those shoes must be of the same pair.

In the first case (<imath>AAABBB</imath>), only one pair is forced to be in the middle. We can choose this pair in <imath>3</imath> ways. There are <imath>2! \cdot 2! = 4</imath> ways to choose the different pairs for the other four shoes in this case, and therefore <imath>3 \cdot 4 = 12</imath> possibilities for this case.

In all of the other cases, we either have <imath>2</imath> or <imath>3</imath> forced pairs <imath>AB</imath>. In all of these cases, there are <imath>3 \cdot 2</imath> or <imath>3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1</imath> ways to choose the different pairs that each shoe belongs to, so <imath>6</imath> cases for each pair.

In total, there are <imath>12+6+6+6=30</imath> cases ignoring if <imath>A</imath> or <imath>B</imath> is left/right. If we now consider these different cases, we will have twice the number of combinations, or <imath>30 \cdot 2 = \boxed{60}</imath> combinations.

~ Phinetium

==Solution 7==

Same thing for solution 1 but you use casework on whether all L's touch or not.
Case 1: All L's touch
24+12=36 possibilities
Case 2: Only 2 L's touch
24 possibilities
36+24=<imath>60</imath>.
